summary_html: Agency **files a court petition** to open a **dependency** (or similar) case. Federal funding frameworks (IV-E/ASFA) link court oversight, reasonable-efforts findings, and permanency timelines to downstream actions.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — court findings; timelines; permanency planning  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal review of court/agency performance measures

provisions_triggered.name: Due Process / Law of the Land

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: In re Department of Family & Protective Services
key_cases.holding: The one-year dismissal deadline in Family Code § 263.401 is mandatory though not jurisdictional, and a trial court that fails to render a final order or a valid extension must dismiss the termination suit.
key_cases.relevance: From the day the petition is filed the Department has one year (plus at most a 180-day extension) to obtain a final order, or the case must be dismissed.
key_cases.quote: We hold that the Family Code required the case to be dismissed and the trial court abused its discretion by failing to do so

key_cases.holding: Service by publication on a parent whose whereabouts were reasonably ascertainable does not satisfy due process under Mullane, and a termination decree so obtained cannot stand.
key_cases.relevance: Controls how DFPS may serve an absent parent when it opens the case; publication is constitutionally inadequate if the parent could have been found with reasonable diligence.
key_cases.quote: Mullane remains the seminal case involving notice by publication, and it explains how to evaluate the adequacy of notice

key_cases.holding: Termination was improper where the mother's relinquishment affidavit was not knowingly and intelligently executed and where the indigent father received no notice of trial and did not waive it.
key_cases.relevance: Once the suit is opened, every parent must receive actual notice of trial, and a relinquishment affidavit signed by a parent who lacks capacity cannot substitute for it.
key_cases.quote: because the father did not receive notice of trial and did not waive notice, we reverse the judgment of the court of appeals

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: A parent's interest in the custody and care of his children is constitutionally protected, and the State may not take children on a presumption of unfitness without a hearing on that parent's actual fitness.
key_cases.relevance: When the Department files its Chapter 262 petition, the parent is constitutionally entitled to an individualized hearing on fitness rather than a status-based presumption.
key_cases.quote: the interest of a parent in the companionship, care, custody, and management of his or her children

key_cases.holding: Ordinary preservation rules apply in parental-termination appeals, so unobjected-to jury charge error is waived, and a trial court must assess whether joint representation creates a substantial risk of conflict between parents.
key_cases.relevance: When the petition names both parents, the court must decide at the outset whether one appointed lawyer can represent both, and the parents must preserve their trial complaints from that point forward.
key_cases.quote: the failure to raise a complaint at trial to a jury charge waives review of that complaint on appeal

key_cases.holding: Only a trial court's failure to extend the Family Code § 263.401 automatic dismissal date before that date passes is jurisdictional; every other claimed defect in complying with § 263.401(b) is non-jurisdictional and must be preserved for appellate review. A docket-sheet pronouncement sufficed to extend the date here, so the final decree was not void.
key_cases.relevance: Once the Department files and the court signs a temporary order, the § 263.401 one-year clock runs; G.X.H. is the current law on which deadline failures kill the trial court's jurisdiction and which merely have to be preserved. It is the case that must travel with In re Dep't of Family & Protective Servs., 273 S.W.3d 637, which construed the pre-2017 statute.
key_cases.quote: The Legislature’s 2017 amendments changed the consequence of expiration of the statutory deadline (without an extension or commencement of the trial) so that it is now jurisdictional.

key_cases.holding: An inmate has no absolute right to appear in person in a civil proceeding; the burden is on the inmate to identify, in the bench-warrant request, the facts showing why his personal appearance is necessary, and a trial court that proceeds without ruling on a request containing no such information does not abuse its discretion.
key_cases.relevance: Once the Department files and the case is set, an incarcerated respondent must affirmatively justify his appearance; the court has no sua sponte duty to produce him.
key_cases.quote: However, an inmate does not have an absolute right to appear in person in every court proceeding.

state_agency.name: Texas Department of Family and Protective Services

notice_requirements.timing: In writing before the department conducts an interview with an alleged perpetrator; the person signs the written notice to acknowledge receipt (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.3091(a))
content_required: That the person may request an administrative review of the department's findings under Tex. Fam. Code § 261.309 (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.3091(a))

Administrative review of a disputed determination of whether child abuse or neglect occurred is conducted by a department employee in administration who was not involved in and did not directly supervise the investigation, and the review must sustain, alter, or reverse the department's original findings (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.309(c))

The review must be conducted as soon as possible but not later than the 45th day after the date the department receives the request, unless the department has good cause for extending the deadline or a related court proceeding or criminal investigation is pending (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.309(d))
notice_requirements.defective_notice_consequence: Not specified in Tex. Fam. Code § 261.3091; the department must document in the case file that it provided the notice (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.3091(b)). A person is not required to exhaust the review remedy before pursuing a judicial remedy provided by law (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.309(e)), and when a finding is overturned the department must remove the person's name from the central registry not later than the 10th business day after it receives notice (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.002(b)(3))
